html:
"Taiwanese Tribes" is the map's label, in 1200, for the indigenous peoples of Taiwan, who speak Austronesian languages. Their ancestors settled the island about 6,000 years ago.

Taiwan matters far beyond its size: most linguists see it as the homeland of the Austronesian language family. From here seafarers moved south to the Philippines (see Austronesians reach the Philippines), and their descendants went on to settle island Southeast Asia, the Pacific and Madagascar.

In 1200 the island had no state. Peoples such as the Atayal, Paiwan, Amis and Bunun lived in villages, growing millet and taro, hunting deer and fishing; some took heads in war. Large Chinese settlement began only in the 1600s, under Dutch Formosa and then Koxinga, and pushed the plains peoples off their land. Today they are about 2 percent of Taiwan's population.
